common_name: Albostriata Chinese Ground Orchid (White-Edged Variegated Hardy Ground Orchid)

planting.note: Plant dormant pseudobulbs 2-3 inches deep in spring after the last frost into rich, well-drained, humus-amended soil in part to full shade; Albostriata is grown chiefly for its crisp white-edged, pleated foliage, which lights up a shaded bed well before the softer pink flower spikes open.

directions: Plant pseudobulbs 2-3 inches deep in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade, where the crisp white leaf margins read almost like a variegated hosta from a distance. Slightly muted magenta-pink flower spikes rise 12-18 inches in late spring, a touch smaller and softer in tone than the species type, since this cultivar's real draw is the season-long foliage display rather than bloom size. Clumps build slowly from the outer pseudobulbs; take divisions from the perimeter rather than splitting the whole crown, and keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since standing water quickly rots the pseudobulbs. In zone 5-6 gardens, apply a loose winter mulch of shredded leaves once foliage dies back.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Siebold's Calanthe (Hardy Yellow Japanese Ground Orchid)

planting.note: Plant pseudobulb divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, moderately acidic, well-drained woodland soil in full to part shade; Siebold's calanthe is one of the few hardy terrestrial orchids with clear yellow flowers and tolerates winters to roughly zone 6b when given a sheltered, well-drained site.

directions: Plant divisions in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained woodland soil in dappled to full shade, treating it much like a shade-loving perennial rather than a houseplant orchid. Broad, glossy, deeply pleated leaves form an attractive clump through the growing season, and upright spikes carry a dozen or more clear soft-yellow flowers with a contrasting lip in mid to late spring, a rare color among cold-hardy terrestrial orchids. It is one of the parent species behind many cultivated hardy Calanthe hybrids and appreciates the same conditions as Calanthe discolor, though it is slightly less cold-tolerant and benefits from a dry winter mulch north of zone 7. Divisions are slow to settle and may skip flowering the first year after transplanting.

common_name: European Lady's Slipper (Common Yellow Lady's Slipper of Eurasia)

planting.note: Plant only laboratory-propagated, nursery-grown rhizomes in fall, set shallowly into humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in dappled shade; European lady's slipper needs cool summers and sharp winter drainage and resents hot, humid conditions.

directions: Plant only tissue-culture-propagated divisions from a reputable specialist grower, setting the rhizome shallowly in humus-rich, neutral-to-alkaline soil that stays cool and evenly moist through spring and summer. This species carries one or two twisted, maroon-brown lateral petals wrapped around a bright canary-yellow pouch in May, the classic combination that made it one of the most sought-after wildflowers of European beech and pine woodlands. It resents heavy clay and prolonged summer heat, so a raised, gritty, leaf-mold-enriched bed in part shade with excellent drainage best mimics the limestone woodland edges it favors in the wild. Because wild populations are legally protected and badly depleted across most of its native range, source stock exclusively from micropropagation labs and never plant wild-collected material.

common_name: Taiwan Lady's Slipper (Formosan Fan-Leaved Lady's Slipper)

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall into humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in part shade; Taiwan lady's slipper is widely regarded as one of the easier Cypripedium species for garden culture, tolerating a wider moisture range than most.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall into humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part shade, mimicking the montane forest floor of Taiwan where this species grows naturally. A single pair of broad, pleated, fan-shaped leaves unfolds each spring, followed by one solitary shell-pink pouch flower veined in deeper rose, opening before most other lady's slippers in the garden. It is one of the fastest of the genus to form multi-stemmed clumps from underground rhizomes, making it a good starting species for gardeners new to growing Cypripedium. Protect emerging shoots from late spring frost with a floating row cover, and keep soil consistently moist through summer without letting it become waterlogged.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall into humus-rich, well-drained garden soil in part shade; Ulla Silkens is a robust interspecific Cypripedium hybrid bred for garden vigor and is notably more forgiving of ordinary border conditions than most species lady's slippers.

directions: Plant nursery-grown rhizomes in fall into humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; this Asian-species hybrid was bred specifically for greater tolerance of typical garden conditions than pure wild Cypripedium species. In late spring it produces clear pink-and-white pouched flowers on sturdy stems well above the foliage, and established clumps push up multiple flowering shoots each year, multiplying faster than most species lady's slippers. It is frequently recommended to gardeners trying Cypripedium for the first time because it tolerates a wider range of soil pH and moisture than fussier wild species while still needing the same basic humus-rich, well-drained shade bed. Mulch lightly over winter in the colder end of its range and avoid disturbing the crown once a clump is established.

common_name: Japanese Egret Flower Orchid (White Egret Orchid)

planting.note: Plant small finger-like tubers 1 inch deep in spring into a constantly moist, acidic, sphagnum-based mix at a pond edge or in a bog container; egret flower orchid goes dormant in winter and the tubers must be kept from both drying out and freezing solid.

directions: Plant small tubers in spring in a constantly moist to boggy, acidic, sphagnum-and-peat-based mix, either at a pond margin or in a shallow container standing in a saucer of water. Through summer, a single slender stem rises to a pure white flower with deeply fringed lateral petals that spread like wings, giving the plant its common name and making it a favorite of Japanese water gardens. Foliage and stem die back completely by autumn, leaving behind a cluster of new offset tubers that should be lifted, stored barely moist and cool, and replanted the following spring in colder parts of its range. Keep the growing medium consistently wet through the growing season, since the plant sits naturally at pond edges and in wet meadows and does not tolerate drying out.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions in spring into consistently moist, sunny meadow or bog-garden soil; Chadds Ford is a selected garden form of nodding ladies' tresses chosen for denser, more strongly spiraled flower spikes than typical wild populations.

directions: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist, sunny meadow, rain-garden, or pond-margin soil, the same open, damp conditions the wild species favors. Chadds Ford was selected for a noticeably denser flower spike with more tightly wound spiraling than typical wild-type nodding ladies' tresses, opening in September and October when few other native perennials are still flowering. Because it is propagated by division and seed rather than wild collection, it establishes more reliably than most native terrestrial orchids and slowly forms small colonies through offset growth. Pair it with native warm-season grasses in a damp meadow planting, and avoid letting the site dry out during summer, since consistent soil moisture is essential to reliable fall bloom.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions in spring into constantly moist, humus-rich meadow or bog soil in full sun to light shade; hooded ladies' tresses is among the most cold-hardy and widely distributed Spiranthes species in North America, ranging from Newfoundland to Alaska and south into cool, wet habitats.

directions: Plant divisions in spring into constantly moist, humus-rich soil in a damp meadow or bog garden in full sun to light shade, conditions that echo the fens, wet prairies, and lakeshores where it grows across its very wide transcontinental range. The tiny white flowers wind up the stem in a single tight spiral rather than the looser multi-ranked spiral seen in some other Spiranthes, opening from mid to late summer. It is one of the most cold-tolerant native orchids in cultivation, surviving into much colder zones than most terrestrial orchids, but it still depends on soil fungi and consistently saturated ground, so a typical dry perennial border is unsuitable. Once established, avoid disturbing the planting, since the fragile roots and their fungal partners are easily damaged by digging nearby.

planting.note: Set out tubers or nursery divisions in early spring into moist, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; robust marsh orchid is one of the largest and easiest Dactylorhiza species for the open border, tolerating ordinary garden soil better than most of its relatives.

directions: Plant tubers or divisions in early spring into moist, humus-rich soil that does not dry out in summer, in a border spot with full sun to part shade. This is the largest commonly grown Dactylorhiza, sending up dense, cylindrical spikes of rich magenta-purple flowers on sturdy stems well above the broad, unspotted basal leaves in late spring and early summer, making a much bolder border statement than the smaller spotted orchids. It tolerates ordinary, moisture-retentive garden soil better than most Dactylorhiza species, which is why it is the one most often offered through mainstream bulb catalogs rather than specialist orchid nurseries. Leave clumps undisturbed once established, top-dress annually with leaf mold, and keep soil consistently moist through the growing season for reliable yearly flowering.
